facts.label: Usage billing units and rates
facts.value: On-Demand is the no-commitment default option. Spot capacity is interruptible and Reserved Instances/Savings Plans require a separate commitment or purchase choice.

facts.label: Usage billing units and rates
facts.value: EC2 Auto Scaling itself has no separate fee, but the instances it launches and CloudWatch monitoring are billed separately.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: New AWS customers can receive up to USD $200 in credits: USD $100 at sign-up and up to another USD $100 through eligible activities. The current FAQ conflicts on expiry: general/advanced-feature sections say six months, while paid-upgrade and earned-credit sections say 12 months.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Under the new Free Plan, account access ends at the earlier of six months after account creation or exhaustion of credits. AWS retains content for 90 days after expiry, then permanently closes the account and deletes content/resources if it is not upgraded.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Legacy accounts created before July 15, 2025 may qualify for the prior 12-month EC2 offer: up to 750 monthly hours on t2.micro, or t3.micro where t2.micro is unavailable, subject to offer limits.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: The new-account EC2 offer lists t3.micro, t3.small, t4g.micro, t4g.small, c7i-flex.large, and m7i-flex.large during the six-month/credit period; usage draws on credits and eligible service limits.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: A separate T4g trial grants all AWS account holders 750 aggregate t4g.small hours per month across Regions through December 31, 2026; unused hours do not carry over, and surplus CPU credits remain chargeable.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: AWS customers get 100 GB/month of internet data transfer out free, aggregated across AWS services and Regions except China and GovCloud.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: EC2 data-transfer-in to AWS is generally free; internet data transfer out is metered, and the post-free-tier rate is tiered and aggregated across listed AWS services.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 internet data transfer out: first 10 TB/month beyond the shared 100 GB AWS free allowance is USD $0.090/GB; next 40 TB is $0.085/GB; next 100 TB is $0.070/GB; above 150 TB is $0.050/GB.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: Transfer between EC2 and another AWS service in the same Region is free in the EC2 FAQ; cross-Region and some cross-AZ/network paths can incur separate transfer charges.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: A NAT Gateway is a separate VPC product with hourly and per-GB processing fees, in addition to EC2 internet egress. A US East (Ohio) pricing example shows USD $0.045/hour and $0.045/GB processing.

facts.label: Build and deployment costs/limits
facts.value: EC2 has no managed source build-minute, preview-build, or deployment quota meter; builders run builds themselves or use a separately billed build/CI service.

facts.label: Build and deployment costs/limits
facts.value: A customer can upload artifacts or run build tools on the instance, but those tasks consume the VM's billed CPU, memory, storage, and network.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Public IPv4 is billed at USD $0.005 per address-hour whether in use or idle, across AWS commercial Regions, including us-east-1; partial hours bill per second with a 60-second minimum.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: EC2's On-Demand page points to VPC pricing for public IPv4; instances in a default VPC can receive public IPv4 addresses by default, while nondefault subnet behavior depends on its setting.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 EBS gp3 storage: USD $0.08/GB-month. The volume includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline performance; extra provisioned IOPS and throughput are priced separately.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 EBS gp3 extra IOPS above the included 3,000: USD $0.005 per provisioned IOPS-month.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 EBS gp3 extra throughput above the included 125 MiB/s: USD $40.96 per GiBps-month (about USD $0.04 per MiB/s-month).

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 EBS gp2 storage: USD $0.10/GB-month.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: The EC2 On-Demand pricing page sends readers to the separate EBS pricing page for attached storage; EBS volume charges continue while an instance is stopped.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Standard EBS snapshots in us-east-1: USD $0.05/GB-month for stored snapshot data.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Load balancers, NAT Gateways, Route 53 domain/DNS, CloudWatch logs, RDS, S3, and AWS Support plans are separate products or services, not included with EC2 compute.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: AWS Budgets can send actual or forecasted cost/usage alerts; budgets without actions are free and two actions-enabled budgets are free.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: AWS Budgets actions can be configured to stop EC2 instances, but this is an opt-in action that needs permissions and configuration; stopping does not stop EBS or public IPv4 charges.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: On the new Free Plan, AWS says the account cannot incur charges while it remains on that plan; it suspends at expiry/exhaustion and access can be restored by upgrading during the stated period.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: Paid-account budgets and billing alerts do not automatically cap all EC2, EBS, network, Marketplace, or tax charges.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: EC2 has no automatic scale-to-zero idle behavior; a running instance is charged even when idle.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: A stopped EBS-backed instance does not incur instance compute or data-transfer usage fees, but attached EBS storage remains billed.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: EC2 Auto Scaling can add or remove instances based on metrics; each running instance incurs EC2 cost, and related CloudWatch metrics/alarms may add charges.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: EC2 has no HTTP request-duration or request-count ceiling imposed by the VM product; limits depend on OS, app, instance capacity, network, and account quotas.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: On-Demand instance quotas are vCPU-based and set per Region; new AWS accounts may start below the published default quota.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: User data has a 16 KB raw limit; instance count and other quotas depend on account and Region.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: Exact account-specific instance quota was not checked because it is account-specific and no login was performed.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: T4g trial eligibility is all new and existing AWS account customers through December 31, 2026, subject to the FAQ's listed Regions; US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 is included.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: For t4g.small's first 750 monthly hours, the trial covers infrastructure cost and waives AMI charge only for Amazon Linux 2, RHEL, and SUSE Quick Start images; applicable AWS Marketplace software fees are excluded.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: Current signup says most new customers need no payment method, but AWS may request one for identity checks; when requested, it can hold USD $1 or equivalent for 3–5 days.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: AWS terms require compliance with sanctions/export laws and representation that the customer and relevant financial institutions are not on prohibited/restricted-party lists. No single current EC2 country-exclusion list was found in the checked public pages.

facts.label: Commercial and acceptable use
facts.value: The Customer Agreement permits use of AWS Services under the agreement and policies; EC2 is a paid commercial service, not a personal-only free hosting plan.

facts.label: Commercial and acceptable use
facts.value: The AWS Acceptable Use Policy prohibits illegal/fraudulent activity, rights violations, serious harm, child sexual exploitation, security abuse, and unsolicited bulk messaging/spam.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: EC2 is infrastructure-as-a-service: customers rent virtual machine instances in AWS Regions and choose an operating system image.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: AWS maintains the physical host and virtualization layer; the customer configures and patches the guest operating system, application, runtime, firewall rules, and app-level backups.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: Instances can be launched directly, through EC2 APIs/CLI, or through other AWS control services. Other services used to build an architecture have separate prices.

facts.label: Suitable app types and directory overlap
facts.value: A customer can install arbitrary compatible software, so EC2 can host websites, APIs, long-running apps, workers, scheduled jobs, and self-managed databases.

facts.label: Suitable app types and directory overlap
facts.value: EC2 is a virtual-machine option in this directory; managed databases, object storage, build platforms, and container orchestration are separate products.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: EC2 instances launch in selectable AWS Regions and Availability Zones; AWS lists 34 Regions in its current regional guide, with some Regions requiring account opt-in.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: The t3 price examples are for US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1; EC2 itself does not include a CDN delivery network.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: EC2 launches a compatible AMI; AWS and third parties publish Linux and Windows images, while customers can build or share their own AMIs.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: A customer can install language runtimes and frameworks on a compatible OS; EC2 does not provide a managed language runtime matrix.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: T3 is x86-64; T4g is Arm64. AMI architecture must match the instance architecture.

facts.label: Framework behavior
facts.value: Common web frameworks can run if the guest OS, architecture, and instance resources support them; server rendering, streaming, framework caching, and adapter behavior are configured by the customer.

facts.label: Framework behavior
facts.value: Managed framework-level deployment or preview behavior is not applicable to raw EC2 instances.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Code can be deployed with SSH/SCP, Git, container tools, user data, AWS CLI, SDK/API, or a customer-built pipeline.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Linux instances support SSH; Windows instances support RDP and AWS-managed connection options.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Launch user data can run shell scripts or cloud-init directives on Linux; raw user data is limited to 16 KB before base64 encoding.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: Long-running workers can run as customer-managed processes or services on an instance; there is no separate EC2 worker feature or per-worker fee.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: Scheduled jobs can use OS tools such as cron or a separate AWS scheduler; EC2 does not include a managed cron control plane.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: EC2 supports customer-configured TCP/UDP networking and public/private interfaces; security groups control inbound and outbound rules at the instance interface.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: HTTP, HTTPS, WebSockets, and streaming protocols can be hosted by software on the VM if allowed through its security group and guest firewall.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Public IPv4 is optional and can change after stop/start; Elastic IP is the persistent-address option and its IPv4 use is separately billed.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Private VPC networking and outbound internet access are configurable; an internet-facing VM may require a public IP or gateway path and corresponding charges.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Long-lived TCP connection behavior can be affected by instance-family connection-tracking limits and timeouts; AWS documents tunable ENI timeouts for supported Nitro instances.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: EBS volumes provide persistent block storage; they remain after a stop/start and can be retained after termination if DeleteOnTermination is disabled.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: Instance-store data is temporary and lost when an instance is stopped, hibernated, terminated, or retired.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: Root volume type is determined by the AMI; the default root EBS volume is deleted on termination unless configured to persist.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: EC2 has no included managed database, cache, queue, or auth service. A customer can self-host these on a VM or connect to separately billed products.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: Self-managed software installed on EC2 remains the customer's responsibility; use of Marketplace AMIs may add vendor software fees.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: EC2 instances can answer for a custom domain using DNS the customer controls; EC2 does not include domain registration.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: HTTPS can be configured on the instance; AWS Certificate Manager says public certificates for standalone EC2 servers should use ACME issuance/renewal directly on the host.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: Automatic public-certificate issuance, renewal, wildcard rules, and app-domain count are not an EC2-managed feature; the selected DNS/ACME/other service determines them.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: EC2 has no branch preview or hosted preview-environment workflow. A customer can create separate instances or use another deploy product.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: Customer deploys through SSH, scripts, user data, image replacement, or their own release tooling; EC2 does not provide application-level rollback.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: Auto Scaling health checks can replace unhealthy instances when configured, but replacement instances and storage are separately billed and the app must be designed for replacement.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: Basic EC2 metrics such as CPU and network are sent to CloudWatch every five minutes and are included in the instance price.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: Guest OS and application logs require customer configuration, commonly the CloudWatch agent; CloudWatch Logs storage/ingestion is billed separately.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: CloudWatch alarms can notify or invoke configured actions; an alert does not itself stop instance billing.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: IAM controls AWS API permissions; an instance profile can give app software temporary role credentials without storing long-term keys on the VM.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: Linux access commonly uses SSH key pairs or Session Manager; Windows access uses RDP or AWS-managed options.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: Security groups act as instance firewalls; AWS advises not to open SSH or RDP to all internet addresses for production.

facts.label: Self-host requirements and ongoing work
facts.value: Self-hosting the EC2 control plane is not applicable; AWS operates the cloud service and physical infrastructure.

facts.label: Self-host requirements and ongoing work
facts.value: Customer remains responsible for guest OS updates, app deployment, server configuration, secrets, capacity, incident response, and backups; AWS account/control-plane outage behavior is not a customer-run controller.

facts.label: Data location and privacy terms
facts.value: AWS Customer Agreement says customers select Regions for content storage; AWS will not move or disclose customer content except as necessary to provide Services or comply with law/order.

facts.label: Data location and privacy terms
facts.value: AWS DPA is incorporated into the Service Terms and applies when customers use AWS Services to process customer data; AWS offers a data processing and transfer framework.

facts.label: Data location and privacy terms
facts.value: The reviewed documents do not promise that all account metadata, operational logs, billing data, support records, or service control-plane data stay in the EC2 workload Region.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: EBS snapshots are point-in-time, incremental backups; they can restore volumes and can be copied across accounts or Regions.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: EBS-backed AMIs capture snapshots of root and attached EBS volumes; these snapshots remain billable until the AMI/snapshots are deregistered/deleted.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager can automate snapshot/AMI schedules, retention, and deletion at no additional policy fee; snapshot storage remains billed.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Instance-store data is not preserved by EBS snapshots unless the customer separately copies it to durable storage.

facts.label: Exit and portability
facts.value: Customer can export data through standard OS/network tools and can create EBS snapshots or AMIs for reuse, copying, or sharing.

facts.label: Exit and portability
facts.value: A running VM does not automatically export its source repository, OS changes, database, or DNS configuration; the customer must maintain independent copies and migration procedures.

facts.label: Exit and portability
facts.value: Closing an AWS account stops new access, but AWS may retain billing and account records as required for legal, security, and business reasons; account closure is not immediate deletion of every record.

facts.label: Product identity and ownership
facts.value: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is AWS's virtual server service.

facts.label: Product identity and ownership
facts.value: The applicable AWS contracting entity depends on the customer's account country.

facts.label: Operating and signup status
facts.value: Active and publicly offered; AWS documents launch steps and on-demand purchasing. No account was created.

facts.label: Operating and signup status
facts.value: AWS account registration requires contact details and phone verification; AWS may ask for a payment method for verification. Most new users can start without a payment method under the current signup path.

facts.label: Availability promise and status history
facts.value: AWS Health Dashboard is the official service-health and event source; it does not establish a historical uptime claim for a particular user's instance.

facts.label: Availability promise and status history
facts.value: The EC2 Instance-Level SLA promises at least 99.5% monthly uptime for an individual instance, with credits of 10%, 30%, or 100% below its listed thresholds.

facts.label: Availability promise and status history
facts.value: The EC2 Region-Level SLA promises at least 99.99% when all running instances are concurrently deployed across two or more AZs in a Region; service credits have separate thresholds.

facts.label: Support channels and terms
facts.value: Basic Support is free and includes 24/7 access to documentation, whitepapers, support forums, and account/billing help; it does not include personalized technical support.

facts.label: Support channels and terms
facts.value: AWS paid support plans offer technical case access and response targets that vary by plan and severity; there is no EC2-only guaranteed response time separate from the account support plan.

facts.label: Support channels and terms
facts.value: EC2 documentation, AWS re:Post/forums, and the AWS Health Dashboard are public self-help/status channels; community responses are not a contractual response commitment.

facts.label: Software license and commercial terms
facts.value: EC2 is a proprietary hosted infrastructure service; an open-source software license for the EC2 service is not applicable.

facts.label: Software license and commercial terms
facts.value: Use for commercial workloads is subject to the AWS Customer Agreement, Service Terms, Acceptable Use Policy, and third-party AMI licenses.

facts.value: AWS ended the legacy 12-month Free Tier offer for accounts created on or after July 15, 2025. New customers use the account Free/Paid plan and up to USD $200 credits; the Free plan ends after six months or credit exhaustion. The new-signup FAQ now gives a six-month credit-expiry answer, but other FAQ sections still say 12 months.

facts.value: Suitable for public websites, APIs, microservices, long-running container workers and finite batch/data-processing tasks; application code is packaged in containers.

facts.label: Suitable app types and directory overlap
facts.value: GPU requests and privileged container mode are unsupported on Fargate; no underlying host access.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: ECS/Fargate is regional compute. Linux coverage includes N. Virginia/Ohio/Oregon, Mumbai/Hyderabad, Singapore/Tokyo/Sydney, Canada, European regions, São Paulo and separately administered China/GovCloud regions.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: Windows and Linux coverage differ; the table restricts some AZ IDs, including Windows in us-east-1 and Linux/Windows in Tokyo and Northern California.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: The June 5, 2026 announcement makes 32-vCPU Linux x86/Arm task sizes available in commercial and GovCloud regions.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: Bring containerized application languages/runtimes rather than choose a managed Node/Python version. Linux images can use other Linux distributions if CPU architecture and required kernel/runtime behavior fit.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: Windows Fargate guides list Windows Server 2019 and 2022 Full/Core on x86; host/platform and image OS versions must match. Windows does not support Fargate Spot, EFS or EBS.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: Current platform tag: Linux LATEST=1.4.0; Windows LATEST=1.0.0. A new revision of a selected platform is adopted by starting/redeploying tasks.

facts.label: Framework behavior
facts.value: Framework packaging/runtime/cache behavior is application-managed inside the container; persistent shared files can use separately configured EFS and network protocols depend on the chosen front door.

facts.label: Framework behavior
facts.value: A provider-maintained framework-version/ISR/image-optimization feature matrix was not found in the generic Fargate architecture, task definition, FAQ or deployment documentation checked.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Supply image URIs in task-definition JSON, register revisions and launch/update through console, AWS CLI/API or infrastructure-as-code; a source directory is not the deployable runtime artifact.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Task execution role permits image pulls/log delivery/secrets retrieval; application task role grants app permissions. Private registry credentials can be supplied through Secrets Manager where required.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Git-based automation is self-configured or an external CI/pipeline integration; AWS now directs former Copilot users toward ECS Express Mode, CDK or adopting generated CloudFormation.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: Long-running worker containers can be maintained as services; standalone tasks serve finite jobs. A Fargate task cannot use the ECS DAEMON scheduling strategy.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: EventBridge Scheduler can launch ECS tasks from rate, cron and one-time schedules, with time-zone options, retries and dead-letter configuration.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: Spot tasks can be interrupted with two minutes' warning; Linux stopTimeout is 30 seconds by default, configurable up to 120 seconds.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Required awsvpc networking gives each task an ENI/private address and security-group controls; public IP assignment/routing or private-subnet NAT/endpoints determine outbound connectivity.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: ALB supports HTTP/HTTPS, WebSockets, HTTP/2 and streaming-compatible connections; NLB is the usual TCP/UDP/TLS front door. Both are separately priced integrations.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: ALB idle timeout defaults to 60 seconds and is configurable from 1 to 4,000 seconds.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: IPv6-only Linux tasks are documented on platform 1.4.0+ in the listed regions; Windows and ECS Exec have IPv6-only restrictions, and IPv4-only dependencies may require DNS64/NAT64.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Fargate architecture overview lists ALB/NLB/Gateway Load Balancer, while the task-networking guide says Fargate services support only ALB and NLB.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: Task-local ephemeral files are erased when the task stops; a bind mount inside that ephemeral allocation does not survive task replacement.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: EFS supports shared persistent files for Linux Fargate platform 1.4.0+, using an additional supervisor container that consumes some task CPU/memory.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: Linux Fargate can attach one newly created EBS volume/task, optionally initialized from a snapshot; existing volumes cannot simply be reattached, and service-task volumes are always deleted at termination.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: Databases, caches, queues, object stores and end-user authentication are separate services: common AWS choices include RDS, S3 and other application integrations.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: C selected dependency: us-east-1 RDS PostgreSQL Single-AZ db.t4g.micro, two burstable vCPUs/1 GiB RAM, US$0.016/instance-hour.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: C storage: RDS PostgreSQL gp3 has a documented 20-GiB minimum; us-east-1 Single-AZ provisioned tariff US$0.115/GB-month. Excess backup storage US$0.095/GB-month.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: Fargate tasks do not provide a universal managed website hostname/certificate: choose a stable front door such as an ALB and configure DNS/custom hostname there.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: Selected ALB HTTPS uses ACM public non-exportable certificate at no certificate charge; DNS-validated eligible in-use ACM certificates can renew automatically.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: ECS native deployment controller supports rolling, blue/green, linear and canary strategies; CodeDeploy-powered blue/green remains a separate documented option.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: Deployment circuit breaker can detect startup/health failures and roll back automatically to a previously COMPLETED deployment when enabled.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: Preview/test environments are additional self-configured services/routes/task revisions, not an included free per-pull-request site pool.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: awslogs can send container stdout/stderr to CloudWatch Logs using task-definition settings and execution-role permissions.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: Basic ECS cluster/service metrics are free; Fargate CPU/memory metrics publish automatically in one-minute periods. Container Insights adds paid per-task/enhanced observability.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: CloudWatch log data is kept indefinitely by default unless a retention policy is set; separate free categories list 5 GB of logs ingestion/archive/query data.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: us-east-1 CloudWatch Standard custom logs: US$0.50/GB ingestion and US$0.03/GB-month stored, before applicable shared free allowances; queries/other features separate.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: CloudWatch Logs supports export to a configured S3 bucket through export tasks; S3 permissions, retention and charges are separate.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: IAM separates deployment permissions, execution roles and application task roles; security groups/network ACLs govern task traffic. MFA is supported and required for traditional AWS root account access.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: Secrets can be referenced from Secrets Manager/SSM or retrieved via application/sidecar design; environment-injected secret changes need a new task/forced deployment to take effect.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: ECS Exec provides opt-in IAM-controlled command/shell access inside a task container, not access to its host. Commands run as root; read-only root filesystems and IPv6-only tasks have restrictions.

facts.label: Self-host requirements and ongoing work
facts.value: Self-host control-plane/server requirements: not applicable to this fully hosted Fargate execution mode. Customer still maintains images, runtime libraries, IAM/networking and data backups.

facts.label: Data location and privacy terms
facts.value: AWS agreement section 1.4 permits selecting content Regions and restricts moving content outside them except for law/binding governmental orders and the stated contract conditions.

facts.label: Data location and privacy terms
facts.value: Customer application content is distinct from personal/account data covered by AWS Privacy Notice, last updated May 18, 2026.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Fargate's temporary filesystem has no persistent backup on task stop. ECS service EBS is deleted at termination; snapshots/EFS/external data need their own backup design.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: C RDS automatic backups provide daily backup-window snapshots/PITR; choose seven-day retention explicitly. DB-instance retention accepts 0–35 days; zero disables automatic backups.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: RDS free backup storage equals 100% of provisioned regional DB storage, allocated across snapshots; changed blocks are incremental and excess usage is billed.

facts.label: Exit and portability
facts.value: Task definitions are JSON and can be described/exported; container images/source are portable artifacts. Keep manifests, image digests and infrastructure configuration outside only the running task.

facts.label: Exit and portability
facts.value: Move persistent EFS/EBS/RDS/object data with their own export/snapshot/backup tools; stopped task scratch space cannot be recovered as a migration backup.

facts.label: Exit and portability
facts.value: Account termination leaves accrued fees payable; ordinary contractual post-termination content retrieval is 30 days subject to exceptions, distinct from Free-plan 90-day upgrade recovery.

facts.label: Product identity and ownership
facts.value: Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate: AWS-managed container execution for the Amazon Elastic Container Service, offered by Amazon Web Services.

facts.label: Product identity and ownership
facts.value: The AWS contracting entity varies by customer location; the current Customer Agreement lists the applicable companies.

facts.label: Operating and signup status
facts.value: Active public offer; no whole-ECS/Fargate shutdown, sunset or acquisition notice found in the official offer, pricing, lifecycle and maintenance sources checked.

facts.label: Operating and signup status
facts.value: Fargate Linux platform 1.3.0 was deprecated June 15, 2026; latest Linux is 1.4.0, latest Windows is its independent 1.0.0.

facts.label: Operating and signup status
facts.value: AWS Copilot CLI support has ended; current ECS notice and March 2026 end-of-support announcement specify June 12, 2026. Older introductory blog banners say May 22, 2026.

facts.label: Availability promise and status history
facts.value: Correct combined ECS/Fargate SLA: 99.99% multi-AZ commitment when tasks are deployed concurrently in at least two AZs; 99.5% single-task/pod commitment.

facts.label: Availability promise and status history
facts.value: SLA credits: 10% below applicable threshold down to 99%, 25% below 99% down to 95%, 100% below 95%; credits must exceed US$1 and claims are due by end of second billing cycle after incident.

facts.label: Availability promise and status history
facts.value: Public AWS Health status endpoint identified, but fetched dashboard body/history was blank and not usable.

facts.label: Support channels and terms
facts.value: Basic support covers account/project/billing access and self-service help; paid Business Support+ provides 24/7 AWS experts, US$29/month minimum or a percentage of account spend, whichever is higher.

facts.label: Support channels and terms
facts.value: Developer Support and old Business Support end January 1, 2027; current docs describe Business Support+ replacement and GovCloud exceptions.

facts.label: Software license and commercial terms
facts.value: Self-hosted service software license: not applicable to hosted ECS on Fargate; AWS agreement, service terms and AUP govern cloud usage.

facts.label: Lifecycle / material Free Tier change
facts.value: AWS ended the legacy 12-month Free Tier offer for accounts created on or after July 15, 2025. New customers use the account Free/Paid plan and up to USD $200 credits; the Free plan ends after six months or credit exhaustion. The new-signup FAQ now gives a six-month credit-expiry answer, but other FAQ sections still say 12 months.

apps.name: Amazon Lightsail
apps.line: Simple virtual servers with separate managed database and container options.

free.text: No repeating free VM tier; AWS credits may apply

work.math: $5 a month for the known server cost. Building from source, domain registration and any outside builder cost extra.
The bundle costs at most $7 a month. Builds and the domain are not in this amount.
$7 for the server + $15 for the database = $22 a month. Builds, the domain and tax are not included.

facts.label: Entry cost and billing terms
facts.value: Lowest current public IPv4 Linux/Unix general-purpose VM bundle: $5 USD/month, US East (Ohio) example scope; includes 0.5 GB RAM, 2 vCPUs, 20 GB SSD, and 1 TB transfer on the current price card.

facts.label: Entry cost and billing terms
facts.value: Lowest Windows VM bundle shown: $9.50 USD/month on the public rate card; its exact AWS Region is not exposed in the page text.

facts.label: Entry cost and billing terms
facts.value: Lightsail VM bundles bill hourly up to the monthly bundle maximum; the published $5 plan rate is $0.0067 USD/hour and $9.50 Windows plan rate is $0.0127 USD/hour.

facts.label: Entry cost and billing terms
facts.value: Stopping an instance does not stop charges. Instance and managed database charges continue until deletion; separate disks, snapshots, IPs, and load balancers can continue charging after instance deletion.

facts.label: Entry cost and billing terms
facts.value: Lightsail’s public price card is in USD; applicable tax is not stated on the price card. AWS terms allow account-specific invoicing/payment currency and regional tax rules.

facts.label: Entry cost and billing terms
facts.value: No Lightsail-specific monthly seat, annual commitment, or minimum contract term is stated on the pricing page.

facts.label: Included compute and storage
facts.value: General-purpose IPv4 Linux bundle examples on the USD card: $5/0.5 GB RAM/2 vCPU/20 GB SSD/1 TB transfer; $7/1 GB/2 vCPU/40 GB/2 TB; $12/2 GB/2 vCPU/60 GB/3 TB. US East (Ohio) is specifically confirmed for the $5 example; other regional mappings are not exposed in the page text.

facts.label: Included compute and storage
facts.value: General-purpose Linux options extend to $24–$1,764 USD/month, with 4–256 GB memory, 2–64 vCPUs, and 80–1,280 GB SSD; exact intermediate configurations are on the public rate card.

facts.label: Included compute and storage
facts.value: Memory-optimized and compute-optimized instance families are separate from general purpose; maximum listed sizes are 512 GB RAM and 72 vCPUs, respectively.

facts.label: Included compute and storage
facts.value: VM plans use SSD system storage; additional detachable Lightsail block storage starts at 8 GB and is charged by allocated capacity.

facts.label: Included compute and storage
facts.value: Lightsail VM CPUs are burstable. They have a baseline CPU level plus a finite burst balance; prolonged high CPU can exhaust burst capacity.

facts.label: Included compute and storage
facts.value: A per-plan CPU architecture or dedicated-core guarantee was not found in the current Lightsail bundle page or instance FAQ.

facts.label: Usage billing units and rates
facts.value: VM compute is billed per hour up to the monthly plan ceiling; deleting earlier prorates by hours used.

facts.label: Usage billing units and rates
facts.value: Data transfer allowance is monthly; inbound and outbound count toward the allowance, while only excess outbound transfer is billed.

facts.label: Usage billing units and rates
facts.value: Container-service hourly charges multiply node power price by scale, with a maximum monthly charge; service bills even when disabled or without a deployment.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: No repeating, perpetual free Lightsail VM tier was found. AWS replaced the legacy 12-month Free Tier for accounts created on or after 2025-07-15 with a credit-funded Free plan; older accounts remain in the legacy cohort. Lightsail-specific trials have separate terms.

facts.label: Ongoing free plan
facts.value: Since 2025-07-15, eligible new AWS accounts can get USD $100 signup credit plus up to USD $100 earned credits and a Free account plan lasting up to six months or credit exhaustion. AWS does not specify a Lightsail-only recurring quota; accounts created before the cutoff remain under legacy terms.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: VM allowance counts both ingress and egress and pools by identical bundle in a Region across instances and IPv4/IPv6; only excess egress to internet/public AWS IP is billable.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: For VM outbound overage, US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada Central, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Paris, Stockholm, and Hong Kong are $0.09 USD/GB; Europe Spain is $0.12 USD/GB.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: VM outbound overage, USD/GB: Mumbai $0.13; Seoul $0.13; Singapore $0.12; Sydney $0.17; Jakarta $0.132; Malaysia $0.108; Tokyo $0.14; São Paulo $0.15.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: The VM transfer allowance is half the listed bundle allowance in Mumbai, Sydney, Jakarta, Malaysia, Hong Kong, and São Paulo.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: Private-IP transfer between Lightsail instances/databases or same-Region AWS resources is free; inbound Lightsail transfer is always free.

facts.label: Data transfer and network costs
facts.value: Container services each include 500 GB/month regardless of node count; excess outbound transfer starts at $0.09 USD/GB and varies by Region.

facts.label: Build and deployment costs/limits
facts.value: Container deployments use an existing Linux image from a public registry or one built locally and pushed using Lightsail tooling. Lightsail publishes no build-minute rate.

facts.label: Build and deployment costs/limits
facts.value: Container service supports up to 10 container entries per deployment and one active deployment at a time.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Attached Lightsail static IPv4 address has no extra charge; a detached address costs $0.005 USD/hour after one hour. IPv6-only instances cannot use static IPv4.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Lightsail load balancer: $18 USD/month on the displayed rate card.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Lightsail block storage: $0.10 USD per allocated GB-month, 8 GB minimum ($0.80 USD/month); 32/64/128/256 GB examples are $3.20/$6.40/$12.80/$25.60 USD/month.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Lightsail snapshots cost $0.05 USD/GB-month of stored data; successive snapshots are incremental for changed data.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Lightsail DNS management includes six zones and unlimited records; first 3 million queries/month are included, then $0.40 USD per million queries.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Domain registration/renewal is billed separately through Route 53; Lightsail FAQ’s linked domain price document dates to December 22, 2021, so current domain prices are not confirmed here.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Optional Lightsail managed database starts at $15 USD/month Standard or $30 USD/month High Availability; these are Lightsail database prices, not Amazon RDS prices.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: Fixed bundle rates cap the compute component at its monthly maximum, but excess data transfer and retained add-ons can raise the invoice.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: AWS account/project spend limits can suspend services or pause/close a project/account at the limit if enabled; the terms do not say this is a default Lightsail-wide spend cap.

facts.label: Protection against a surprise bill
facts.value: Lightsail supports billing alerts/monitoring, but no hard, default per-instance invoice cap that prevents all overages was found.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: VM bundles are fixed-size; to change to a larger VM, create a snapshot and a new instance at the larger bundle. No automatic VM autoscaling policy is published for Lightsail Instances.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: Container service nodes can be scaled up to 20 and power/scale can be changed without downtime.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: Standard VM keeps billing while stopped; a container service stays billed when disabled or empty.

facts.label: Scaling, sleeping, and idle billing
facts.value: No Lightsail VM scale-to-zero or idle-sleep rule was found.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: Lightsail account quota: default maximum 20 instances per supported Region; it is adjustable, and new accounts may begin with lower quotas.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: Container service quota: 20 nodes, 10 entries per deployment, 50 saved deployment versions, and 4 days of container logs; quota table notes new accounts may start lower.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: Load balancer guidance: up to 5 GB/hour, 400,000 new connections/hour, and 15,000 concurrent active connections; consistently higher traffic may degrade or throttle.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: No published HTTP request-count, per-request execution-time, or concurrency limit was found for raw VM instances.

facts.label: Runtime and request limits
facts.value: Lightsail database instance sizes include 1–32 GB memory; lowest 1 GB class has a specific managed-database SLA exclusion.

facts.label: Other unavoidable or easy-to-miss charges
facts.value: Separate Lightsail container service node rates on the USD card are $7/$10/$15/$40/$80/$160 per node/month (Nano through XLarge); exact region selection is not exposed in the text view.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: Lightsail-specific trial terms remain inconsistent after the 2025-07-15 AWS Free Tier change: the billing FAQ says old short-term trials are unavailable to new Lightsail customers and that trials begun before removal run to their end; the same FAQ says new customers get one month free on a $15 managed database plan, while the Lightsail free page advertises selected 90-day trials. The general AWS change does not erase already-started trial terms.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: Lightsail Getting Started still describes the $5 USD instance plan as free for one month, up to 750 hours, with one free month credited. After the 2025-07-15 AWS Free Tier transition, the current billing FAQ says earlier short-term trials are unavailable to new Lightsail customers and only trials started before removal continue to their original end date; the guide does not state a cutoff or whether new users still qualify.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: The Lightsail free page still advertises 90-day offers for selected Linux/Windows instance, container and database plans, despite the AWS Free Tier change effective 2025-07-15 and current billing FAQ saying old short-term trials are unavailable to new customers. Its page does not state all eligibility conditions or explain the mismatch.

facts.label: Trial and buyer requirements
facts.value: AWS account needs a valid email and payment method; the Lightsail FAQ says most major credit cards are accepted. Country-specific signup exclusions were not fully enumerated in pages checked.

facts.label: Commercial and acceptable use
facts.value: Commercial use is supported; AWS describes reselling Lightsail instance plans as a use case.

facts.label: Commercial and acceptable use
facts.value: AWS AUP bans illegal/fraudulent activity, rights violations, security attacks, child sexual abuse material, and unsolicited mass email/spam, among other restrictions.

facts.label: Commercial and acceptable use
facts.value: Lightsail terms prohibit using the service to avoid charges on other AWS services, including traffic proxying or excessive processing through load balancing/CDN; AWS may throttle data services or suspend an account.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: Lightsail Instances are virtual private servers (VPSs) running in AWS Regions. The customer controls the guest OS and app.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: Lightsail also sells managed Linux container services, managed MySQL/PostgreSQL databases, block disks, buckets, load balancers, DNS, and CDN distributions. These are separate Lightsail line items.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: For VMs, AWS supplies the virtual infrastructure and blueprint image; the customer installs, updates, patches, secures, and operates the OS and app after launch.

facts.label: Hosting and management model
facts.value: Container services are infrastructure-managed; customers supply and maintain Linux container images and app configuration.

facts.label: Suitable app types and directory overlap
facts.value: Suitable for public websites, web apps/APIs, self-managed long-running services, development stacks, and packaged server apps.

facts.label: Suitable app types and directory overlap
facts.value: Arbitrary code can run on an instance if the customer installs and operates its dependencies.

facts.label: Suitable app types and directory overlap
facts.value: Container service accepts Linux container images; Windows-based containers are not supported.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: Lightsail is available in 19 listed Regions: Ohio, N. Virginia, Oregon, Canada Central; Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Paris, Spain, Stockholm; Hong Kong, Jakarta, Malaysia, Mumbai, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo; São Paulo.

facts.label: App server and delivery regions
facts.value: VM and container app compute run in the selected AWS Region; availability zones are selectable within that Region where offered.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: VM supports the OS/app runtime installed by the customer; available blueprint families include Amazon Linux, AlmaLinux, CentOS Stream, Debian, FreeBSD, openSUSE, Ubuntu, and Windows Server, subject to retired-image notices.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: Lightsail-packaged app blueprints include WordPress, WordPress Multisite, LAMP, Nginx, and Node.js. Additional Marketplace AMIs are supported for eligible products.

facts.label: Languages, runtimes, and architecture
facts.value: Container service supports Linux-based Docker images; Windows containers are not supported.

facts.label: Framework behavior
facts.value: A Lightsail VM can run a framework installed by the customer; AWS does not publish managed framework adapters or feature guarantees for SSR, streaming, or cache revalidation.

facts.label: Framework behavior
facts.value: Container frameworks run if packaged into a supported Linux image and meet container service limits; no framework-specific compatibility matrix was found.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: VM deploy options include OS/app blueprint, Marketplace AMI, instance image/snapshot, launch script, and manual SSH/RDP administration.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Container service accepts locally pushed images or public registry images; AWS CLI and Lightsail tools are documented.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: No native Lightsail GitHub/GitLab repository auto-deploy workflow is documented; CodeDeploy/CodePipeline is a separate AWS deployment path with separate service terms/costs.

facts.label: Deployment inputs and tools
facts.value: Container Linux images only; Windows is supported as a local build machine, not as the deployed container OS.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: VM can run background workers and scheduled jobs through OS-level software the customer installs and operates.

facts.label: Workers and scheduled jobs
facts.value: Container services run containerized app processes, but the public docs do not promise a dedicated scheduled-job scheduler or separate worker role.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: VM offers public IPv4/IPv6, private IPv4, outbound network access, and customer-configured port rules; instance firewall rules support TCP/UDP and IPv4/IPv6.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Lightsail supports dual-stack or IPv6-only instance plans; not every blueprint supports IPv6-only.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Lightsail VM networking supports private traffic with same-Region Lightsail resources and AWS resources through VPC peering; peering requires a default VPC.

facts.label: Network and connection support
facts.value: Container service public endpoints support HTTPS over IPv4/IPv6; they do not expose TCP/UDP public endpoints, and one container is the public endpoint.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: VM system disk persists while instance exists, but is deleted with the instance; AWS recommends attached block storage and snapshots for data requiring stronger durability.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: Attached block disks persist independently and can move between instances; max one disk 16 TB, 20 TB total per account, up to 15 disks per instance.

facts.label: Persistent app files
facts.value: Container local writable filesystem persistence across replacement/redeploys is not promised in the checked container docs; persist important data in a database, bucket, or external storage.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: Managed database option includes MySQL and PostgreSQL, with Standard and High Availability plans; AWS operates the underlying OS/infrastructure and scheduled maintenance.

facts.label: Databases and supporting services
facts.value: Lowest published Lightsail DB: $15 USD/month Standard, 1 GB RAM, 1 processor, 40 GB SSD, 100 GB transfer; High Availability starts at $30 USD/month.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: Customer can map a registered custom domain through Lightsail DNS or another DNS host; domain registration is separate.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: Lightsail load balancers, container services, and CDN distributions support managed TLS certificates for validated domains; certificates are free with a load balancer.

facts.label: Domains and encrypted connections
facts.value: Load-balancer certificate allows up to 10 names and no wildcard names; container service uses up to four custom domains.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: VM release is customer-controlled (SSH/scripts/CLI/API); Lightsail does not supply branch previews or source-based rollback.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: Container releases save the latest 50 deployment versions; a previous version can be redeployed in the same service.

facts.label: Preview, release, and recovery workflow
facts.value: VM snapshots can restore to a new instance; they are not an in-place rollback and do not restore an external database automatically.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: VM console has resource metrics including CPU, network, status checks, and burst capacity; metrics are retained for 15 days at 1-minute resolution and 63 days at 5-minute resolution.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: Metric alarms evaluate at five-minute intervals and can notify in console, email, or SMS; up to two alarms per metric.

facts.label: Logs and basic monitoring
facts.value: Container service exposes CPU/memory metrics and stdout/stderr logs; logs are kept for four days, with no container-metric alarm support documented in its FAQ.

facts.label: Access and secret handling
facts.value: AWS account credentials provide Lightsail console access; IAM roles/policies can grant scoped Lightsail permissions; MFA is recommended.

facts.label: Container and runtime qualifications

Internal credentials could have exposed secret environment variables in 1,022 projects; Appwrite found no evidence those variable values were read, but incomplete provider audit logs prevent ruling it out.

facts.label: Self-host controller outage detail

facts.label: Platform disaster recovery versus customer copies
facts.value: Security docs describe internal infrastructure backups: some databases PITR seven days, others four-hour backups retained seven days. Deployment retention/downloads are separate.

facts.label: Exit path
facts.value: Keep own Git source; download retained deployment source code or build output before cleanup. Database direct PostgreSQL connections permit standard client access; owned domains can point elsewhere.

facts.label: Deletion and downgrade
facts.value: Account deletion is available in Console; privacy allows legal-record retention/public activity persistence. Pro-to-Free downgrade applies Free restrictions at term end.

facts.label: Product identity and ownership
facts.value: Appwrite Sites, a product of Appwrite. Privacy policy identifies the company as Appwrite Code Ltd.

facts.label: Operating and signup status

facts.label: Uptime agreement
facts.value: SLA docs: Free none; Pro 99.5%, Scale 99.9%, Enterprise 99.95% monthly for services actively used.

facts.label: Support channels

The November 4 report confirms one customer’s function code/logs were accessed and code changed briefly; secret environment variables in 1,022 projects were potentially reachable, but Appwrite found no evidence the values were read and could not rule it out. Appwrite says the flaw and exposed credentials were fixed.
